title: 73 Beef Cattle Calving School improves producer confidence in calving management
content:
Abstract
Calving management can be a complicated subject for both seasoned and beginning cattle producers. A workshop entitled Beef Cattle Calving School was held on May 17, 2024 at the Mississippi State University Animal and Dairy Sciences Building in Starkville, MS. The objective of this one-day workshop was for beef cattle producers and extension agents to enhance their knowledge of beef cattle reproduction by exploring topics directly related to the calving process. These topics included reproductive anatomy and calving stages, dystocia prevention, providing assistance at calving, newborn calf management, injuries and diseases associated with calving, and case studies. Speakers included Extension specialists and veterinarians from the Mississippi State University College of Veterinary Medicine. Connecting attendees with veterinarians proved to be very effective in facilitating discussion and addressing producers’ concerns with their past experiences as well as hypothetical scenarios. The workshop also included demonstrations with beef cattle reproductive tracts, a life size calf dummy, calf snare, and calving chains. Participants were provided with an evaluation after the course to rate the topics and speakers, ascertain their anticipated economic benefit of implementing strategies from the workshop, and to what they attribute these benefits. They also reported demographic information, how they learned about the program, suggestions for improvement, and the most important or beneficial thing they learned from the workshop. There were 28 participants in the workshop, of which 25 submitted anonymous evaluations of the program. Both large and small herds were represented with 17 participants indicating ownership of less than 100 animals and 9 participants reporting 101-500 animals. All topics and speakers received a rating of 5 from the majority of respondents on a 1 to 5 scale indicating excellent topic relevance and speaker effectiveness. Participants represented 14 Mississippi counties and one Alabama county. Regarding economic impact, 16 respondents indicated that they anticipated a benefit while four respondents selected “N/A” and another chose “no impact.” Including multiple topics related to calving proved to be impactful as respondents reflected on the most important or beneficial thing they learned. Each of the topics covered had a positive comment related to them, with multiple participants stating “all.” Proper calving chain placement, how to hold the chain, and repositioning of calves as demonstrated with the calf dummy stood out to several participants as well. Overall, the workshop was well received with positive feedback, and each of the respondents indicated they would be likely to very likely to recommend Mississippi State University as a contact on beef cattle.
